why: If RL changes how each step is computed rather than writing a format readout, the base-RL lens difference peaks where the computation goes wrong, so about half of 90 peaks sit at the first wrong step.
Accuracy rises in proportion to dose with no plateau, so a=0.25 adds a quarter of the 410 -> ~462 cued gap: 410 + 13.
Proportional dose response: a=0.5 adds half the ~52-point cued gap to 410.
Proportional dose response: a=0.75 adds three quarters of the ~52-point cued gap to 410.
With no saturation or collapse along the full-rank change, extrapolating to a=1.5 continues the linear rise past RL's ~462, held below 500 by the hardest problems.
The theory puts no saturation point at or just past a=1, so a=1.5 produces almost no degenerate word-salad endings.
Proportional dose response on the plain prompt: 224 + 0.25 x (463 - 224).
Proportional dose response on the plain prompt: 224 + 0.5 x (463 - 224).
Length moves with the size of the full-rank change, so a=0.25 moves a quarter of the way from the cued base's 3,933 to RL's ~4,690 mean tokens.
Magnitude of the full-rank change carries much of the effect, so a random difference of matched norm gives most of the cued gap, as the random edit did in the Qwen check.
A 432-right cell that loses about 18 of the base's right answers to resampling must fix about 40 of the 90 problems the cued base got wrong.
The a=0.5 cell at ~436 right, losing about 15 base-right problems to resampling, fixes about 41 of the base's 90 wrong problems.
Format and length are a side effect separate from accuracy and come only with RL's own full-rank pattern, so a random matched-norm difference keeps the cued base's ~3,933 mean tokens.
The change is high-rank and depends on the input, so one constant vector per layer, which can only carry a fixed readout shift, closes little of KL on cued-base text.
Same input-dependent, high-rank change on RL text: a constant per-layer vector closes only a small share.
A constant on the MLP output alone captures even less of an input-dependent change than the full-layer constant on cued-base text.
A constant MLP-output vector on RL text captures only a small fixed part of the input-dependent MLP change.
The function is concentrated in a small neuron set acting through Olmo's outlier channels, missed by first-order rankings, so the 472 always-on neurons close far more than their 0.13 % share.
The same concentrated always-on set closes a larger share on RL text, where KL closure runs about 1.3x higher than on cued-base text in every earlier arm.
